narrative:
The model estimates a 53% chance that you will leave your current job. Because this probability tips above 50%, the system recommends denying your promotion to reduce the risk of investing in someone likely to depart soon.

Three factors drove this prediction, ranked by importance. First, having received other job opportunities while at the company strongly pushed the model toward predicting you will leave. Employees predicted to stay rarely report outside offers, so this signal carried the heaviest weight. Second, your overall career experience of more than 11 years also increased the likelihood of leaving. While most employees the model expects to stay have only 1–5 years of total experience, your longer track record makes departure more probable in the eyes of the system. Third, your six to ten years spent in this specific organization worked in the opposite direction, modestly pulling the prediction back toward staying. Most stayers have shorter tenure here, so your loyalty to the current employer slightly offset the other signals.

Taken together, the combination of external opportunities and your senior overall experience outweighed your solid tenure with us, tipping the balance toward expected turnover.

The organization should discuss retention measures with you, such as clearer advancement paths or addressing any unmet needs the external offers may reflect. You may want to reflect on whether your long-term goals still align with staying. Understanding these drivers can help both sides decide on the best next step. (248 words)
